content: Ventouse is a vacuum device designed to assist in the delivery of a baby when labor has not progressed sufficiently. It serves as an alternative to forceps delivery. However, it is generally not used when the baby is in the breech position or in cases of premature births. This method is also referred to as vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery. During the procedure, the woman is positioned in the lithotomy position and actively participates by pushing. A suction cup is applied to the baby’s head, and suction is used to draw the scalp into the cup. Most ventouse devices are equipped with handles, which allow the practitioner to guide the baby’s head during delivery. Once the baby’s head is delivered, the device is detached, enabling the mother to complete the delivery process. In some cases, ventouse deliveries have been performed before the cervix is fully dilated, though there is debate among medical professionals regarding the appropriateness of this practice. If the ventouse attempt is unsuccessful, a cesarean section may be required to deliver the baby. There are three primary indications for the use of a ventouse during delivery: 1. Prolonged pushing during the second stage of labor or maternal exhaustion. 2. Fetal emergencies during the second stage of labor, often indicated by changes in the fetal heart rate. 3. Compared to other forms of assisted delivery, ventouse has several advantages. It typically does not require an episiotomy and causes minimal internal bruising. Additionally, the mother remains actively involved in the birthing process. The force applied to the baby’s head is generally less than that used in forceps delivery, which reduces the likelihood of significant marks on the baby’s head and face. However, there are also disadvantages associated with ventouse delivery. The baby may develop a temporary swelling on the head, known as a chignon, due to the suction. Additionally, the baby may experience distress as a result of the strong suction applied to the head.
